svg.title: Follow-up schedules after NMIBC and after bladder preservation
svg.desc: Schematic comparing the follow-up schedules of the two roads in two columns. The left column is non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (Ta / T1 / CIS) under the EAU 2026 guideline; every recommendation carries the strength Weak and the guideline itself notes a lack of RCTs. One cell is not stratified: the first cystoscopy is always three months after TURBT, level of evidence 1a. Low risk: month 3, month 12, then yearly, with a stopping point after five years; the wording is "should be considered", not "stop". This stratum has no urinary cytology and no routine imaging, and a negative haematuria dipstick has negative predictive values of 0.89 and 0.94. Intermediate risk excluding high grade: month 3, six-monthly for two years, then yearly, with a stopping point after ten years; the high-grade subgroup within intermediate risk is followed as high risk. High and very high risk: three-monthly for two years, six-monthly to five years, then yearly, marked life long with no stopping point, because "Recurrences after ten years tumour-free are not unusual"; cytology runs at the same frequency as cystoscopy. High and very high risk carries a second axis, upper-tract CT urography: yearly to five years, two-yearly to ten years, also life long with no stopping point. The ten-year rate of upper-tract tumour ranges from 1.9% in T1 tumours to 25% in multiple recurrent high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer, and reached 3.6% within ten years for high-risk patients (Ta G3 and CIS) in a population-based study. The right column is the bladder kept after trimodality therapy: three guidelines, three schedules, all three ending with no stopping point. EAU 2026: three-monthly cystoscopy for two years, six-monthly to year five, yearly thereafter, with cytology and chest, abdominal and pelvic CT or MRI including the upper tract every six to twelve months for the first three to five years. AUA / ASCO / SUO: three-monthly in year one, every four to six months in year two, every six to twelve months thereafter, with imaging six-monthly for the first two years and the guideline noting that no published data show that this frequency improves survival. NICE guideline NG2: rigid cystoscopy three months after radiotherapy, three-monthly for two years, six-monthly for the next two years, yearly thereafter, with upper-tract imaging yearly for five years. The intervals differ but all three end at "yearly thereafter"; not one reaches a stop. Two Taiwan lines at the foot: National Health Insurance item 28019C, cystoscopy, 1,800 points; and no entry found for any cap on the number of cystoscopies in follow-up, where zero hits means no entry was found rather than "not reimbursed", so ask the hospital medical affairs office or your case manager. Three closing questions: which stratum am I in or which guideline schedule am I on, does my schedule have a stopping point, and do I need upper-tract CT every year.

g.text: FOLLOW-UP SCHEDULES - WHICH CELLS HAVE A STOPPING POINT AND WHICH DO NOT
Two roads, two follow-up schedules: which cells stop, and
which never do
On the left, after resection of non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer. On the right, after trimodality therapy has finished and the
bladder has been kept. The risk strata, the intervals and the stopping points differ; no figure may be carried from one side to
the other.
The hatched red cells mean one thing only: the guideline gives no stopping point. Cystoscopy in high and very high risk is
life-long, and so is upper-tract CT urography.
Left column - non-muscle-invasive disease (Ta / T1 /
CIS): after resection
EAU Guidelines on Non-muscle-invasive Bladder Cancer, 2026 edition. The
schedule follows the risk stratum assigned at diagnosis, not how clean this
particular cystoscopy looked.
This cell is not stratified: the first cystoscopy is always at
month three
“should always be performed three months after TURBT in all patients with
TaT1 tumours and CIS”
EAU Guidelines on Non-muscle-invasive Bladder Cancer, 2026 edition, level of
evidence 1a
It is not merely one more test. What is seen at month three changes the rhythm
of everything that follows, and may change the treatment. So this one is not
moved back.
Low risk
Small, single, low-grade Ta
Month 3
Month 12
Yearly thereafter
A stopping point after five years
The guideline wording is "should be considered" - stopping cystoscopy, or
moving to a less invasive method, should be considered; it does not say "stop".
This stratum has no urinary cytology and no routine imaging; the same passage
reports negative predictive values of 0.89 and 0.94 for a negative haematuria
dipstick in low-risk cohorts.
"Five years and you can stop" belongs to this stratum and to no other.
Intermediate risk (high grade excluded)
The box that holds both ends
Month 3
Six-monthly for two years
Yearly thereafter
A stopping point after ten years
Lower-intensity follow-up on the basis of one small randomised trial, to ten
years.
One line is often dropped: the high-grade subgroup within intermediate risk is
followed as high risk.
High and very high risk
Cytology at the same frequency as cystoscopy
Three-monthly for two years
Six-monthly to five years
Yearly thereafter
Life long - no stopping point
The guideline gives its reason in one sentence: "Recurrences after ten years
tumour-free are not unusual." In this stratum, a recurrence after ten clear
years is not a curiosity.
The strategy for this stratum is intensive early cystoscopy and cytology, plus
life-long follow-up.
Upper tract (high / very high risk)
CT urography, a separate axis
Yearly to five years
Two-yearly to ten years
Life long as well - no stopping point
The figures with denominators: the ten-year rate of upper-tract tumour varies
widely between populations, from 1.9% in T1 tumours to 25% in multiple
recurrent high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer; in one
population-based study, high-risk patients (Ta G3 and CIS) reached 3.6% within
ten years.
A clean bladder does not mean a clean urinary tract.
Every recommendation in this column carries the strength
Weak
The guideline says so itself: the follow-up recommendations rest mainly on
retrospective data, and there is "a lack of RCTs" on whether the frequency of
surveillance cystoscopy can safely be reduced.
This is not a regulation. It is the best arrangement currently available, and the
people who propose it say the evidence behind it is not strong.
Right column - the bladder that was kept: after
trimodality therapy
Three guidelines, three schedules, and the intervals differ. That is not a
typographical error, and merging them into one is not something to do.
EAU 2026
Muscle-invasive and Metastatic Bladder Cancer guideline
Three-monthly cystoscopy for two years
Six-monthly to year five
Yearly thereafter
No stopping point
Most recurrences occur two to five years after treatment; this section is
expert consensus. Urinary cytology and chest, abdominal and pelvic CT or MRI
(including the upper tract) every six to twelve months for the first three to five
years, and as clinically indicated thereafter.
AUA / ASCO / SUO
American urological and oncological societies
Three-monthly in year one
Every four to six months in year two
Every six to twelve months thereafter
No stopping point
Imaging is recommended six-monthly for the first two years, and the same
passage adds a sentence of its own: no published data show that this imaging
frequency improves survival.
NICE guideline NG2
Bladder cancer: diagnosis and management
Rigid cystoscopy three months after radiotherapy
Three-monthly for two years
Six-monthly for the next two years
Yearly thereafter
No stopping point
Upper-tract imaging yearly for five years.
The intervals differ, but all three end at "yearly thereafter" -
not one of them reaches a stop.
So "a few more years and I can stop" has nothing behind it on this road. Ask
your doctor to point at one of the three schedules and write it down.
Taiwan (both roads): the line that was found, and the line that was not
National Health Insurance schedule of medical service benefits: item 28019C,
cystoscopy, 1,800 points.
Whether there is a cap on the number of cystoscopies in a follow-up setting: no
entry found in the remarks column. Zero hits means no entry was found, not
"definitely not reimbursed" - ask the hospital medical affairs office or your case
manager, and do not infer it yourself.
Three sentences to say out loud at the next clinic visit
Which stratum am I in (or which guideline schedule am I on)?
Does my schedule have a stopping point?
Do I need upper-tract CT every year?
Schematic, redrawn from the EAU Guidelines on Non-muscle-invasive Bladder Cancer (2026 edition), the EAU Guidelines on Muscle-invasive and Metastatic Bladder Cancer
(2026), the AUA/ASCO/SUO guideline, NICE guideline NG2 and the Taiwan National Health Insurance schedule of medical service benefits; not reproduced from any
published figure. Populations, designs and endpoints differ between studies, so the points are not directly comparable.
